63	The risk of all-cause injury and site-specific injury in
64	athletes after concussion: A systematic review and meta-
65	analysis
66	Mingyu Liao1, Yue Gu 2, Keyin Liu1*
67	1
68	  Department of Physical Training, Institute of Aviation Safety and Security,
69	
70	China Civil Aviation Flight Academy, Chengdu 610000, China
71	
72	2
73	    Department of Otorhinolaryngology, Upper Airway Inflammation and Tumor
74	
75	Laboratory, The First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University,
76	
77	Chongqing, China
78	
79	
80	                                                               S
81	* Corresponding author E-mail: lky5208888@163.com
82	
83	Contributing authors: 13637931865@163.com; 943758506@qq.com
84	                                                           E S
85	Abstract:                                          PR
86	                                             IN
87	                             E
88	Objective: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the risk
89	
90	
91	                         C L
92	                        I
93	of subsequent all-cause, recurrent concussion, upper extremity, and lower
94	
95	                      T
96	                   A R
97	extremity injuries in athletes with a history of sport-related concussion.
98	
99	Methods:    Following   PRISMA      guidelines,   cohort   studies   published   from
100	
101	inception through August 2025 were retrieved from PubMed, Cochrane Library,
102	
103	Embase, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The methodological quality of included
104	
105	studies was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Pooled odds
106	
107	ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-
108	
109	effects models. Pre-specified subgroup and meta-regression analyses were
110	
111	conducted to investigate sources of heterogeneity, including injury timing, study
112	
113	design, sport type, and athlete competition level.
114	
115	
116	
117	                                         1
118	                               ARTICLE IN PRESS
119	
120	
121	
122	Results: Nineteen cohort studies involving 86,879 athletes were included.
123	
124	Athletes with a history of concussion had significantly higher odds of
125	
126	sustaining a subsequent all-cause injury (OR=1.93; 95% CI=1.39– 2.68). The
127	
128	risk was most pronounced for recurrent concussion (OR=3.06; 95% CI=1.81–
129	
130	5.17), and was also significantly elevated for upper extremity (OR=1.76; 95%
131	
132	CI=1.10– 2.81) and lower extremity injuries (OR=1.49; 95% CI=1.06– 2.09).
133	
134	Given the high heterogeneity observed in the primary outcomes (I2 > 90%),
135	
136	the pooled effect sizes should be interpreted with caution as average
137	
138	associations across varying study contexts, rather than as precise predictions
139	
140	
141	                                                            S S
142	                                                          E
143	applicable to all settings. Subgroup analysis revealed that injury risk was
144	
145	
146	                                                   PR
147	statistically significant in studies with follow-up periods beyond six months
148	
149	
150	                                              IN
151	(OR=1.94) but not for shorter durations. The association was strongest and
152	
153	                            L E
154	                         IC
155	statistically significant among college athletes (OR=2.29; 95% CI=1.53– 3.44),
156	
157	
158	                      RT
159	while estimates for professional and high school athletes were not significant.
160	                    A
161	Meta-regression identified sport type as a significant moderator of injury risk
162	
163	(p=0.038).
164	
165	Conclusion: A history of concussion significantly increases the risk of
166	
167	subsequent injuries, with the odds being highest for recurrent concussion. The
168	
169	persistence of this risk beyond six months suggests that clinical recovery does
170	
171	not equate to full functional recovery. These findings underscore the need for
172	
173	enhanced     return-to-play   protocols   that   incorporate   objective   functional
174	
175	assessments and targeted rehabilitation to mitigate the heightened vulnerability
176	
177	
178	
179	                                          2
180	                               ARTICLE IN PRESS
181	
182	
183	
184	to injury in post-concussed athletes.
185	
186	Keywords: Concussion; Sports injuries; Upper extremity injury; Lower extremity
187	
188	injury; Athletes; Meta-analysis
189	
190	
191	
192	
193	1. INTRODUCTION
194	Concussion, a form of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), is caused by direct
195	
196	or indirect forces to the head, resulting in neurological and cognitive symptoms
197	
198	(Scorza & Cole, 2019). It presents with a range of neurological and cognitive
199	
200	symptoms and has become a major public health issue. In the United States alone,
201	
202	
203	                                                              S S
204	millions of concussions are estimated to occur each year[1]. Systematic reviews and
205	
206	                                                            E
207	                                                     PR
208	meta-analyses have shown that concussion is common across many sports. One study
209	
210	
211	                                               IN
212	found an overall concussion rate of 0.23 per 1,000 athlete exposures in youth sports,
213	
214	
215	                            L E
216	                          C
217	with the highest rates seen in high-risk activities such as American football and ice
218	
219	                       T I
220	                      R
221	hockey [2, 3]. However, actual incidence rates are likely much higher due to
222	
223	                    A
224	underreporting and athletes often hiding symptoms[4], further emphasizing the scale of
225	
226	the problem.
227	
228	  Returning to sport too soon after a concussion can increase the risk of further injury.
229	
230	Studies consistently show that athletes with a history of concussion are more likely to
231	
232	experience future musculoskeletal injuries, especially in the lower limbs[5]. This
233	
234	increased risk is thought to result from lasting impairments in balance, proprioception,
235	
236	and neuromuscular control, which may continue even after clinical symptoms have
237	
238	resolved[6, 7]. ‘Clinical recovery,’ as discussed in this study and related literature,
239	
240	is traditionally operationally defined as the resolution of self-reported symptoms
241	
242	                                           3
243	                                ARTICLE IN PRESS
244	
245	
246	
247	and the return of routine clinical physical examination findings to baseline
248	
249	levels[8]. These deficits can reduce an athlete’s ability to coordinate movement, stabilize
250	
251	joints, and maintain posture[9]. The underlying causes likely involve complex changes
252	
253	in how the brain processes sensory and motor signals[10]. Other factors—such as age,
254	
255	sex, and hormone levels—may also influence recovery and risk after repeated
256	
257	concussions[11]. Although these findings point to a link between concussion and later
258	
259	injury, the full extent of the risk, its consistency across athlete populations, and how it
260	
261	affects different body regions remain unclear[12].
262	
263	  Most previous reviews have focused on specific sports or injury types, potentially
264	
265	
266	                                                               S S
267	missing the broader patterns of injury risk among diverse athlete groups[13]. Given the
268	                                                             E
269	                                                      PR
270	growing research and ongoing publication of new studies, an updated and comprehensive
271	
272	
273	                                                 IN
274	meta-analysis is essential. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the
275	
276	                             L E
277	                           C
278	overall and site-specific risk of injury in athletes following a concussion. The goal is to
279	                          I
280	                       RT
281	support better-informed prevention strategies, improve post-concussion care, and guide
282	
283	                     A
284	safer return-to-play decisions.
285	
286	
287	2. METHOD
288	This meta-analysis followed the PRISMA 2020[14] guidelines for transparent
289	
290	and standardized reporting. The study protocol was registered in advance with
291	
292	PROSPERO        (CRD420251044641)          to    ensure    methodological     rigor    and
293	
294	transparency.
295	
296	2.1 Data sources and searches
297	
298	A comprehensive and systematic literature search was conducted on August 9,
299	
300	2025, across five major electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane
301	
302	                                             4
303	                                ARTICLE IN PRESS
304	
305	
306	
307	Library, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The search encompassed all literature
308	
309	from the inception of each database through the date of the search. This
310	
311	review was restricted to articles published in the English language.
312	
313	The search strategy was structured around four core concepts to ensure the
314	
315	precise retrieval of relevant studies: (1) exposure (concussion/mild traumatic
316	
317	brain injury); (2) outcome (all types of subsequent injuries); (3) population
318	
319	(athletes); and (4) association (risk).
320	
321	To ensure a comprehensive search, each core concept combined subject
322	
323	headings (e.g., MeSH terms, Emtree) with keywords (i.e., free-text terms). For
324	
325	
326	                                                              S S
327	the exposure concept, search terms included the subject heading "Brain
328	                                                            E
329	                                                      PR
330	Concussion" as well as the keywords "Concussion*," "Commotio Cerebri," and
331	
332	
333	                                               IN
334	"Mild Traumatic Brain Injury." The outcome concept was searched using the
335	
336	                             L E
337	                           C
338	subject heading "Wounds and Injuries" and the keywords "Injur*," "Wound*,"
339	                          I
340	                       RT
341	and "Trauma*." The study population was defined by the subject heading
342	
343	                     A
344	"Athletes" and the keyword "Athlete*." To enhance the specificity for
345	
346	epidemiological studies, the association concept utilized the subject heading
347	
348	"Risk" and the keyword "Risk*."
349	
350	Within each conceptual group, the respective search terms were combined using
351	
352	the Boolean operator "OR." Subsequently, the four core concepts were
353	
354	combined using the "AND" operator. The complete, detailed search strategies
355	
356	for   all   five   databases   are   available   in   the   supplementary   materials
357	
358	(Supplementary Table S1, S2, S3, S4 and S5). In addition, a rigorous manual
359	
360	
361	
362	                                           5
363	                            ARTICLE IN PRESS
364	
365	
366	
367	search of the reference lists of all included studies and relevant systematic
368	
369	reviews was performed to identify any potentially eligible articles that may
370	
371	have been missed.
372	
373	2.2 Eligibility criteria
374	
375	Studies meeting the following criteria were eligible for inclusion: (1) Study
376	
377	Design: The investigation must be a retrospective or prospective cohort study.
378	
379	(2) Participants and Exposure: The study population must consist of athletes,
380	
381	with the exposure of interest being a history of concussion. (3) Outcomes: The
382	
383	study assessed the risk of subsequent injury. The primary outcome was defined
384	
385	
386	                                                        S S
387	as "all-cause injury," encompassing all new injuries sustained during sports
388	                                                      E
389	                                                 PR
390	participation, including acute/overuse and contact/non-contact injuries, while
391	
392	
393	                                            IN
394	explicitly excluding non-sport-related illnesses and general medical conditions.
395	
396	                            L E
397	                          C
398	Secondary outcomes included recurrent concussion, upper extremity injury, and
399	                         I
400	                      RT
401	lower extremity injury. (4) Data Reporting: To be included, a study must have
402	
403	                    A
404	reported effect estimates— such as an odds ratio (OR), relative risk (RR), or
405	
406	hazard ratio (HR)—with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the
407	
408	association between concussion and the specified injury outcomes, or provided
409	
410	sufficient raw data to calculate these metrics. Exclusion criteria comprised
411	
412	conference abstracts, narrative reviews, meta-analyses, study protocols, and case
413	
414	reports. To address potential data overlap in studies utilizing the same database
415	
416	(e.g., NCAA, NFL), priority was given to the publication with the largest
417	
418	sample size or longest follow-up period to prevent statistical bias. Finally,
419	
420	
421	
422	                                        6
423	                               ARTICLE IN PRESS
424	
425	
426	
427	studies that did not report relevant outcomes or lacked extractable data for
428	
429	effect size calculation were excluded.
430	
431	2.3 Study selection
432	
433	Two reviewers (MYL and YG) independently screened studies based on
434	
435	predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The process began with a review of
436	
437	titles and abstracts to exclude duplicates and clearly irrelevant studies. Full
438	
439	texts of potentially eligible articles were then assessed to confirm final
440	
441	eligibility. Disagreements were resolved through consultation with a third
442	
443	reviewer (KYL) to reach consensus.
444	
445	2.4 Risk of bias
446	                                                              S S
447	                                                            E
448	                                                     PR
449	The methodological quality of each included cohort study was evaluated using the
450	
451	
452	                                                IN
453	Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS)[15]. This scale assesses three key areas: participant
454	
455	
456	                              L E
457	                            C
458	selection and exposure assessment (maximum of 4 points), comparability between study
459	
460	                         T I
461	                        R
462	groups (maximum of 2 points), and outcome assessment along with adequacy of follow-
463	
464	                      A
465	up (maximum of 3 points). Based on the total score, studies were categorized as low
466	
467	quality (0–3 points), moderate quality (4–6 points), or high quality (7–9 points).A total
468	
469	of 19 cohort studies were included in this analysis. The detailed NOS scores for
470	
471	each study are presented in (Supplementary Table S6). All included studies
472	
473	scored between 7 and 9 points, and were consequently judged to be of high
474	
475	methodological quality, indicating a low overall risk of bias.
476	
477	2.5 Statistical analysis
478	
479	All statistical analyses for this systematic review and meta-analysis were
480	
481	performed using R (v4.4.1 or later), primarily with the metafor, forestplot,
482	
483	                                            7

1324	          A
1325	4.1 Principal findings
1326	
1327	This meta-analysis, encompassing 19 cohort studies and 86,879 athletes,
1328	
1329	provides robust evidence that a history of concussion is a significant risk
1330	
1331	factor for subsequent injuries. Our primary finding reveals that athletes who
1332	
1333	have sustained a concussion are nearly twice as likely to experience a
1334	
1335	subsequent all-cause injury compared to their non-concussed counterparts (OR =
1336	
1337	1.93, 95% CI: 1.39– 2.68). The risk was most pronounced for recurrent
1338	
1339	concussions, with previously concussed athletes facing a threefold greater odds
1340	
1341	of   sustaining   another   concussion   (OR   =   3.06,   95%   CI:   1.81– 5.17).
1342

1345

1349	
1350	elevated odds for both upper extremity (OR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.10–2.81) and
1351	
1352	lower extremity injuries (OR = 1.49, 95% CI: 1.06–2.09).

athletes after concussion: A systematic review and meta-
analysis
Mingyu Liao1, Yue Gu 2, Keyin Liu1*

                                                           E S
Abstract:                                          PR
                                             IN
                             E
Objective: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to quantify the risk


                         C L
                        I
of subsequent all-cause, recurrent concussion, upper extremity, and lower

                      T
                   A R
extremity injuries in athletes with a history of sport-related concussion.

Methods:    Following   PRISMA      guidelines,   cohort   studies   published   from

inception through August 2025 were retrieved from PubMed, Cochrane Library,

Embase, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The methodological quality of included

studies was evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Pooled odds

ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-

effects models. Pre-specified subgroup and meta-regression analyses were

conducted to investigate sources of heterogeneity, including injury timing, study

design, sport type, and athlete competition level.



                                         1
                               ARTICLE IN PRESS



Results: Nineteen cohort studies involving 86,879 athletes were included.

Athletes with a history of concussion had significantly higher odds of

sustaining a subsequent all-cause injury (OR=1.93; 95% CI=1.39– 2.68). The

risk was most pronounced for recurrent concussion (OR=3.06; 95% CI=1.81–

5.17), and was also significantly elevated for upper extremity (OR=1.76; 95%

CI=1.10– 2.81) and lower extremity injuries (OR=1.49; 95% CI=1.06– 2.09).

Given the high heterogeneity observed in the primary outcomes (I2 > 90%),

the pooled effect sizes should be interpreted with caution as average

associations across varying study contexts, rather than as precise predictions


                                                            S S
                                                          E
applicable to all settings. Subgroup analysis revealed that injury risk was


                                                   PR
statistically significant in studies with follow-up periods beyond six months


                                              IN
(OR=1.94) but not for shorter durations. The association was strongest and

                            L E
                         IC
statistically significant among college athletes (OR=2.29; 95% CI=1.53– 3.44),


                      RT
while estimates for professional and high school athletes were not significant.
                    A
Meta-regression identified sport type as a significant moderator of injury risk

(p=0.038).

Conclusion: A history of concussion significantly increases the risk of

subsequent injuries, with the odds being highest for recurrent concussion. The

persistence of this risk beyond six months suggests that clinical recovery does

not equate to full functional recovery. These findings underscore the need for

enhanced     return-to-play   protocols   that   incorporate   objective   functional

assessments and targeted rehabilitation to mitigate the heightened vulnerability



                                          2
                               ARTICLE IN PRESS



to injury in post-concussed athletes.

Keywords: Concussion; Sports injuries; Upper extremity injury; Lower extremity

injury; Athletes; Meta-analysis




1. INTRODUCTION
Concussion, a form of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), is caused by direct

or indirect forces to the head, resulting in neurological and cognitive symptoms

(Scorza & Cole, 2019). It presents with a range of neurological and cognitive

symptoms and has become a major public health issue. In the United States alone,


                                                              S S
millions of concussions are estimated to occur each year[1]. Systematic reviews and

                                                            E
                                                     PR
meta-analyses have shown that concussion is common across many sports. One study


                                               IN
found an overall concussion rate of 0.23 per 1,000 athlete exposures in youth sports,


                            L E
                          C
with the highest rates seen in high-risk activities such as American football and ice

                       T I
                      R
hockey [2, 3]. However, actual incidence rates are likely much higher due to

                    A
underreporting and athletes often hiding symptoms[4], further emphasizing the scale of

the problem.

  Returning to sport too soon after a concussion can increase the risk of further injury.

Studies consistently show that athletes with a history of concussion are more likely to

experience future musculoskeletal injuries, especially in the lower limbs[5]. This

increased risk is thought to result from lasting impairments in balance, proprioception,

and neuromuscular control, which may continue even after clinical symptoms have

resolved[6, 7]. ‘Clinical recovery,’ as discussed in this study and related literature,

is traditionally operationally defined as the resolution of self-reported symptoms

                                           3
                                ARTICLE IN PRESS



and the return of routine clinical physical examination findings to baseline

levels[8]. These deficits can reduce an athlete’s ability to coordinate movement, stabilize

joints, and maintain posture[9]. The underlying causes likely involve complex changes

in how the brain processes sensory and motor signals[10]. Other factors—such as age,

sex, and hormone levels—may also influence recovery and risk after repeated

concussions[11]. Although these findings point to a link between concussion and later

injury, the full extent of the risk, its consistency across athlete populations, and how it

affects different body regions remain unclear[12].

  Most previous reviews have focused on specific sports or injury types, potentially


                                                               S S
missing the broader patterns of injury risk among diverse athlete groups[13]. Given the
                                                             E
                                                      PR
growing research and ongoing publication of new studies, an updated and comprehensive


                                                 IN
meta-analysis is essential. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to assess the

                             L E
                           C
overall and site-specific risk of injury in athletes following a concussion. The goal is to
                          I
                       RT
support better-informed prevention strategies, improve post-concussion care, and guide

                     A
safer return-to-play decisions.


2. METHOD
This meta-analysis followed the PRISMA 2020[14] guidelines for transparent

and standardized reporting. The study protocol was registered in advance with

PROSPERO        (CRD420251044641)          to    ensure    methodological     rigor    and

transparency.

2.1 Data sources and searches

A comprehensive and systematic literature search was conducted on August 9,

2025, across five major electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane

                                             4
                                ARTICLE IN PRESS



Library, Web of Science, and EBSCO. The search encompassed all literature

from the inception of each database through the date of the search. This

review was restricted to articles published in the English language.

The search strategy was structured around four core concepts to ensure the

precise retrieval of relevant studies: (1) exposure (concussion/mild traumatic

brain injury); (2) outcome (all types of subsequent injuries); (3) population

(athletes); and (4) association (risk).

To ensure a comprehensive search, each core concept combined subject

headings (e.g., MeSH terms, Emtree) with keywords (i.e., free-text terms). For


                                                              S S
the exposure concept, search terms included the subject heading "Brain
                                                            E
                                                      PR
Concussion" as well as the keywords "Concussion*," "Commotio Cerebri," and


                                               IN
"Mild Traumatic Brain Injury." The outcome concept was searched using the

                             L E
                           C
subject heading "Wounds and Injuries" and the keywords "Injur*," "Wound*,"
                          I
                       RT
and "Trauma*." The study population was defined by the subject heading

                     A
"Athletes" and the keyword "Athlete*." To enhance the specificity for

epidemiological studies, the association concept utilized the subject heading

"Risk" and the keyword "Risk*."

Within each conceptual group, the respective search terms were combined using

the Boolean operator "OR." Subsequently, the four core concepts were

combined using the "AND" operator. The complete, detailed search strategies

for   all   five   databases   are   available   in   the   supplementary   materials

(Supplementary Table S1, S2, S3, S4 and S5). In addition, a rigorous manual



                                           5
                            ARTICLE IN PRESS



search of the reference lists of all included studies and relevant systematic

reviews was performed to identify any potentially eligible articles that may

have been missed.

2.2 Eligibility criteria

Studies meeting the following criteria were eligible for inclusion: (1) Study

Design: The investigation must be a retrospective or prospective cohort study.

(2) Participants and Exposure: The study population must consist of athletes,

with the exposure of interest being a history of concussion. (3) Outcomes: The

study assessed the risk of subsequent injury. The primary outcome was defined


                                                        S S
as "all-cause injury," encompassing all new injuries sustained during sports
                                                      E
                                                 PR
participation, including acute/overuse and contact/non-contact injuries, while


                                            IN
explicitly excluding non-sport-related illnesses and general medical conditions.

                            L E
                          C
Secondary outcomes included recurrent concussion, upper extremity injury, and
                         I
                      RT
lower extremity injury. (4) Data Reporting: To be included, a study must have

                    A
reported effect estimates— such as an odds ratio (OR), relative risk (RR), or

hazard ratio (HR)—with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the

association between concussion and the specified injury outcomes, or provided

sufficient raw data to calculate these metrics. Exclusion criteria comprised

conference abstracts, narrative reviews, meta-analyses, study protocols, and case

reports. To address potential data overlap in studies utilizing the same database

(e.g., NCAA, NFL), priority was given to the publication with the largest

sample size or longest follow-up period to prevent statistical bias. Finally,



                                        6
                               ARTICLE IN PRESS



studies that did not report relevant outcomes or lacked extractable data for

effect size calculation were excluded.

2.3 Study selection

Two reviewers (MYL and YG) independently screened studies based on

predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The process began with a review of

titles and abstracts to exclude duplicates and clearly irrelevant studies. Full

texts of potentially eligible articles were then assessed to confirm final

eligibility. Disagreements were resolved through consultation with a third

reviewer (KYL) to reach consensus.

2.4 Risk of bias
                                                              S S
                                                            E
                                                     PR
The methodological quality of each included cohort study was evaluated using the


                                                IN
Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS)[15]. This scale assesses three key areas: participant


                              L E
                            C
selection and exposure assessment (maximum of 4 points), comparability between study

                         T I
                        R
groups (maximum of 2 points), and outcome assessment along with adequacy of follow-

                      A
up (maximum of 3 points). Based on the total score, studies were categorized as low

quality (0–3 points), moderate quality (4–6 points), or high quality (7–9 points).A total

of 19 cohort studies were included in this analysis. The detailed NOS scores for

each study are presented in (Supplementary Table S6). All included studies

scored between 7 and 9 points, and were consequently judged to be of high

methodological quality, indicating a low overall risk of bias.

2.5 Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses for this systematic review and meta-analysis were

performed using R (v4.4.1 or later), primarily with the metafor, forestplot,

                                            7
                            ARTICLE IN PRESS



dplyr, and ggplot2 packages.

2.5.1 Effect Size Calculation and Pooling

The primary effect measure was the odds ratio (OR). To minimize confounding

bias, priority was given to adjusted odds ratios (aORs) derived from

3.3 Risk of All-Cause Injury associated with history of concussion

Nineteen cohort studies were included to assess the link between a history of concussion

and the risk of subsequent all-cause Injury[17-35]. Substantial heterogeneity was

observed across studies (I² = 94.4%, p < 0.001), prompting the use of a random-effects

faced a significantly higher risk of later injury compared to those without (OR = 1.93,

95% CI: 1.39–2.68; p < 0.001) (Figure 2). This suggests that a prior concussion may

be associated with an approximately 93% increased risk of sustaining a subsequent

sports-related injury.

          A
4.1 Principal findings

This meta-analysis, encompassing 19 cohort studies and 86,879 athletes,

provides robust evidence that a history of concussion is a significant risk

factor for subsequent injuries. Our primary finding reveals that athletes who

have sustained a concussion are nearly twice as likely to experience a

subsequent all-cause injury compared to their non-concussed counterparts (OR =

1.93, 95% CI: 1.39– 2.68). The risk was most pronounced for recurrent

concussions, with previously concussed athletes facing a threefold greater odds

of   sustaining   another   concussion   (OR   =   3.06,   95%   CI:   1.81– 5.17).

                                         24
                              ARTICLE IN PRESS



Furthermore, the risk extended to other body regions, with significantly

elevated odds for both upper extremity (OR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.10–2.81) and

lower extremity injuries (OR = 1.49, 95% CI: 1.06–2.09).

4.2 Comparison with Prior Evidence and Novel Insights

The principal findings of this meta-analysis are consistent with and build upon

the existing body of literature, strengthening the evidence base for the

association between concussion and subsequent injury risk. Our pooled estimate

for all-cause injury (OR=1.93) aligns remarkably well with the landmark meta-

analysis by Mcpherson et al (2019)[36], which reported that concussed athletes


                                                            S S
had over two times greater odds of sustaining a subsequent musculoskeletal injury
                                                          E
                                                    PR
(MSKI) (OR=2.11). Similarly, our finding of a 49% increased risk for lower


                                               IN
extremity injury (OR=1.49) is comparable to other recent systematic reviews. For

                            L E
                          C
instance, Jildeh et al (2022)[37] reported an odds ratio of 1.85 for LE injury
                         I
                      RT
within one year of concussion, and Mccann et al (2022b)[38] found a 58% greater

                    A
risk (RR=1.58) specifically in college athletes. Furthermore, the threefold

increased risk for recurrent concussion (OR=3.06) strongly corroborates the well-

established principle that a prior concussion is the single greatest predictor for a

future one [39]. This estimate is quantitatively similar to the findings of van Ierssel

et al (2021)[40], who reported a pooled risk ratio of 3.64 for recurrent

concussion in children and adolescents.

  Beyond corroborating previous work, the present study offers several novel

insights derived from our detailed subgroup and meta-regression analyses. A



                                          25
                                 ARTICLE IN PRESS



key new finding is the identification of sport type as a significant moderator

of all-cause injury risk (meta-regression p=0.038). This suggests that the risk

profile for athletes in contact sports may differ from that of athletes in cohorts

that   include   participants    from   non-contact   sports,   potentially   reflecting

differences in exposure to high-impact forces or sport-specific movement

patterns. Our subgroup analysis also revealed a nuanced picture across

competition levels. The risk was most pronounced and statistically significant

among college athletes (OR=2.29), whereas the estimates for professional

(OR=1.40) and high school athletes (OR=2.03) did not reach statistical


                                                             S S
                                                           E
significance. This heterogeneity in findings across levels is not a contradiction


                                                      PR
but a critical insight. The strong signal in collegiate sports may be attributable


                                               IN
to the high-quality, systematic injury surveillance systems common in large

                            L E
                         IC
NCAA programs, which reduce measurement error and increase statistical


                      RT
power. Conversely, the non-significant finding in professional athletes could be
                    A
multifactorial, stemming from superior, individualized rehabilitation, a "survivor

bias" where only the most robust athletes compete [41], or smaller study

sample sizes. At the high school level, the lack of statistical significance is

likely due to methodological noise, as inconsistent injury reporting and high

variability in athlete maturation and care introduce significant heterogeneity (I2

=94.4%), obscuring a clear statistical signal.

  The study also explored how injury risk evolves over time. While prior work

suggested increased risk within 90 days [42] , our analysis indicates that the



                                          26
                             ARTICLE IN PRESS



increase in risk was statistically significant in studies with follow-up periods

exceeding six months (OR=1.94), whereas the association did not reach

statistical significance in studies with shorter follow-up durations (<6 months;

p=0.087). It is important to note that this is an observational finding. It

suggests that within existing cohort studies, susceptibility to injury following

concussion may not resolve immediately upon the cessation of short-term

clinical symptoms, but rather remains observable over a more extended

temporal window. This implies that the underlying neuromuscular deficits

driving this elevated risk are not transient but persistent, manifesting as injuries


                                                           S S
                                                         E
during prolonged athletic exposure, thereby challenging the traditional notion of


                                                   PR
"rapid recovery." The prevailing hypothesis regarding the mechanism of this


                                              IN
increased risk is that subtle, sub-clinical neurological deficits persist in athletes

                            L E
                         IC
even after they are clinically deemed "recovered" following symptom resolution


                      RT
and standard return-to-play assessments [43]. These deficits include impaired
                    A
neuromuscular and postural control, where concussion disrupts the brain's

processing of visual, vestibular, and somatosensory information, leading to

altered gait, diminished stability, and delayed reaction times [44]. Given that

traditional clinical evaluations often fail to detect these subtle functional

impairments, the Amsterdam International Consensus Statement and recent

studies strongly advocate for the implementation of objective, standardized

assessment tools [45]. For instance, the ImPACT test can be utilized to detect

delays in cognitive reaction time, while the Sway or Balance Error Scoring



                                         27
                               ARTICLE IN PRESS



System (BESS) serves to assess postural stability [46, 47]. Relying solely on

symptom resolution without validation from these objective tools may fail to

identify latent neuromuscular deficits that are sufficient to increase the risk of

subsequent injury. Furthermore, altered sensorimotor integration and cognitive

deficits may leave athletes with insufficient cognitive resources to maintain

proper movement mechanics during complex competitive scenarios, thereby

exacerbating injury risk [48].

4.3 Clinical and Preventive Implications

Recovery from concussion often extends beyond the resolution of symptoms, with


                                                              S S
ongoing neuromuscular and balance deficits that increase the risk of re-injury[49, 50].
                                                            E
                                                     PR
These findings support extending post-concussion monitoring beyond six months and


                                                IN
adopting individualized rehabilitation plans focused on restoring motor control, balance,

                             L E
                           C
and cognitive-motor integration[6, 51, 52]. High-risk groups—especially professional
                          I
                       RT
athletes—may benefit from interventions such as biomechanical screening and

                     A
neurocognitive-motor training[53, 54]. Comprehensive assessment strategies that

include physical, cognitive, and psychosocial evaluations can guide more effective

treatment plans[55]. Recent evidence also suggests that early reintroduction of physical

activity, rather than prolonged rest, may promote faster recovery[56, 57]. Proven

approaches include aerobic exercise[58], cognitive rehabilitation, and vestibular

therapy[59]. Return-to-play (RTP) decisions should account for the increased risk of

MSK injury[60]. Incorporating neuromechanical assessments into RTP protocols can

help ensure athletes are physically ready to resume competition. Ongoing injury



                                           28
                              ARTICLE IN PRESS



surveillance—particularly in contact sports—along with educational programs

promoting symptom reporting, is essential to preventing reinjury and addressing

underreporting of concussion[61].


5. STRENGTHS, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
The credibility of this meta-analysis is supported by several methodological

strengths. The study was conducted in strict adherence to the PRISMA 2020

guidelines   and   was   pre-registered   with     PROSPERO      (CRD420251044641),

ensuring methodological transparency and minimizing the risk of reporting bias.

A comprehensive search strategy was executed across five major electronic


                                                                S S
databases, supplemented by manual reference checks, to ensure a thorough and
                                                              E
                                                    PR
representative sample of the available literature. The inclusion of 19 cohort


                                               IN
studies with a large pooled sample of 86,879 athletes provides substantial

                            L E
                          C
statistical power and enhances the generalizability of the findings. Furthermore,
                         I
                      RT
we employed robust statistical methods, including a random-effects model

                    A
appropriate for heterogeneous data, and conducted leave-one-out sensitivity

analyses that confirmed the stability of our results. Crucially, by using

subgroup and meta-regression analyses, this study moved beyond a simple

pooled estimate to actively investigate potential sources of heterogeneity.

Finally, formal testing with Egger’ s regression ( p=0.051) and visual

inspection of the funnel plot revealed no significant evidence of publication

bias, further strengthening confidence in the results.

  Despite    the   aforementioned     strengths,    several    limitations   must   be



                                          29
                               ARTICLE IN PRESS



acknowledged. First, a high degree of statistical heterogeneity was observed in

the analysis of all-cause injury (I2 = 94.4%). Although meta-regression

identified sport type as a significant moderator, residual heterogeneity suggests

that the pooled effect sizes should be interpreted as average associations across

varying study contexts, rather than as uniform predictive values applicable to

all settings. Second, while nearly three-quarters (73.7%) of the included studies

adjusted for critical confounders such as prior injury history— and sensitivity

analyses confirmed the stability of the results— the inclusion of unadjusted

studies (n=5) and inconsistencies in covariate selection across studies may still


                                                                 S S
                                                               E
introduce potential bias. Third, the robustness of evidence for certain subgroups


                                                        PR
is limited; the assessment of upper extremity injury was based on only two


                                                  IN
studies, and the lack of significant risk observed in professional and high

                             L E
                          IC
school athlete subgroups is more likely attributable to insufficient statistical


                       RT
power or methodological discrepancies rather than an absence of risk; thus, it
                     A
should not be inferred that these populations are risk-free. Finally, heterogeneity

in   the   definitions   of   "concussion"        and   "injury,"   potential   unmeasured

confounders, and language bias resulting from restricting the search to English-

language literature may affect the precision of the effect estimates. Future research

should prioritize large-scale, multinational, prospective cohort studies utilizing

standardized definitions to further elucidate causal relationships and optimize

prevention strategies.


6.CONCLUSION


                                             30
                               ARTICLE IN PRESS



In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis provides robust

evidence that athletes with a history of concussion face a significantly elevated

risk of sustaining various subsequent injuries. The findings explicitly indicate

that symptom resolution does not equate to full functional recovery. Although

athletes may appear symptom-free, objective assessment tools— such as the

ImPACT or Sway tests— may reveal persistent neuromuscular deficits that do

not fully resolve despite the cessation of reported symptoms. Consequently,

relying solely on symptom clearance as the benchmark for "clinical recovery"

may fail to accurately reflect an athlete's true functional status. A window of


                                                               S S
                                                             E
heightened vulnerability to injury persists for a prolonged period after athletes


                                                      PR
are cleared to return to play under current standard protocols. Accordingly,


                                                 IN
these results support the refinement of existing concussion management

                             L E
                          IC
protocols, particularly the integration of scientifically validated, objective


                       RT
functional assessments, to ensure full recovery prior to return-to-play and to
                     A
mitigate the risk of subsequent injury. Adopting such a comprehensive strategy

is essential for safeguarding the short- and long-term health of athletes.

Journal of Sports Sciences, December 2007; 25(14): 1557 – 1566




The role of a short post-lunch nap in improving cognitive, motor,
and sprint performance in participants with partial sleep deprivation


J. WATERHOUSE, G. ATKINSON, B. EDWARDS, & T. REILLY

Research Institute for Sport and Exercise Sciences, Liverpool John Moores University, Liverpool, UK

Abstract
The aim of this study was to determine the effects of a post-lunch nap on subjective alertness and performance following
partial sleep loss. Ten healthy males (mean age 23.3 years, s ¼ 3.4) either napped or sat quietly from 13:00 to 13:30 h after a
night of shortened sleep (sleep 23:00 – 03:00 h only). Thirty minutes after the afternoon nap or control (no-nap) condition,
alertness, short-term memory, intra-aural temperature, heart rate, choice reaction time, grip strength, and times for 2-m and
20-m sprints were recorded. The afternoon nap lowered heart rate and intra-aural temperature. Alertness, sleepiness, short-
term memory, and accuracy at the 8-choice reaction time test were improved by napping (P 5 0.05), but mean reaction
times and grip strength were not affected (P 4 0.05). Sprint times were improved. Mean time for the 2-m sprints fell from
1.060 s (sx ¼ 0.018) to 1.019 s (sx ¼ 0.019) (P ¼ 0.031 paired t-test); mean time for the 20-m sprints fell from 3.971 s
(sx ¼ 0.054) to 3.878 s (sx ¼ 0.047) (P ¼ 0.013). These results indicate that a post-lunch nap improves alertness and aspects
of mental and physical performance following partial sleep loss, and have implications for athletes with restricted sleep during
training or before competition.

Keywords: Sleep loss, athletic performance, fatigue, daytime sleep

   "abstract":"The study tested whether a 30-minute post-lunch nap improves alertness and performance after a night of shortened sleep.    "tldr":"In 10 healthy young men with one night of shortened sleep, a 30-minute afternoon nap improved alertness, memory and short-sprint times compared with quiet rest. The study is small and used non-athletes, so it suggests a possible benefit for athletes but does not prove it.",
   "methods":"Crossover laboratory study of 10 healthy males (mean age 23.3 years) who slept 4 hours less than usual the night before testing. In the nap condition they rested in bed from 13:00 to 13:30; in the control they read quietly. Thirty minutes later they completed alertness and sleepiness scales, a digit-span memory test, an 8-choice reaction time test, handgrip strength and three 2 m and 20 m sprints, with heart rate and aural temperature recorded.",
   "findings":"The nap lowered heart rate and aural temperature and improved subjective alertness (t9 = 5.77, p < .001) and sleepiness (t9 = 6.74, p < .001).    "limitations":"The study had 10 male participants, none described as athletes, and tested only one nap length at one time of day.    "practicalImplications":"A 30-minute lunchtime nap after restricted sleep may improve alertness and short-sprint times in healthy adults, so it is worth trialling for athletes who lose sleep.    "athleteDev":"A short afternoon nap could be tested as a readiness tactic on days after restricted sleep, with sprint times and alertness checked against a no-nap day. The result comes from non-athletes, so the effect should be confirmed in the squad before it becomes routine.",
   "rtp":"The study does not address injured athletes or return to sport and cannot be used to judge return-to-sport readiness."

24	is gaining increasing attention, as these injuries represent a major concern for athletes’
25	health and performance. This narrative review explores the role of speciﬁc genetic variants,
26	such as those in ACE, ACTN3, AMPD1, VDR, and APOE, in predisposing athletes to injury.
27	In parallel, the emerging role of microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-133a, miR-208a, and
28	miR-214 in regulating gene expression related to muscle regeneration, inﬂammation, and
29	neuroprotection, is highlighted. These small noncoding RNAs are inﬂuenced by environ-

79	Introduction
80	The predisposition to injury and sports performance is primarily determined by intrinsic
81	biological traits, including genetic polymorphisms that inﬂuence muscle structure, bone
82	density, and neuromuscular function. While training and other extrinsic factors can
83	modulate injury risk, they do not deﬁne the baseline predisposition, which is rooted in
84	these intrinsic characteristics.
85	    The Healthy Injury-Free Adolescent Athletes study has shown that multiple factors,
86	including biomechanical, environmental, and psychosocial aspects, contribute signiﬁ-
87	cantly to injury risk in young athletes.1 Similarly, studies on Olympic athletes have
88	demonstrated that elite-level performance tends to run in families, emphasizing the
89	important contribution of genetic background.2 Foundational studies further suggest
90	that up to 60–70% of the variability in physiological adaptations to physical activity
91	(such as VO2max and strength gains) and injury susceptibility may be explained by gen-
92	etic factors.3 Engaging in intense physical activity comes with an increased risk of injur-
93	ies, the nature and severity of which vary depending on the sport. Indeed, each sport has a
94	speciﬁc risk proﬁle, related to its unique physical and technical demands. Nearly 70% of
95	track and ﬁeld athletes experience injuries per season.4 Lower limb injuries are extremely
96	common in certain sports, affecting 50% of athletes participating in football, marathon,
97	triathlon, gymnastics (female), basketball, pole vaulting, rugby sevens, volleyball
98	(female), handball, and tennis.5 Among these injuries, muscular injuries such as ham-
99	string strains are particularly prevalent; for instance, professional footballers experience
100	a 20% hamstring injury rate per season, with 20% of these progressing to a chronic stage.6
101	Stress fractures and stress reactions, while less frequent, pose a greater challenge due to
102	their longer recovery periods, with athletes requiring on average 67.4 days (± 73.1) to
103	return to full training for stress reactions, and up to 199 days (± 205.2) for stress frac-
104	tures.7 In comparison, concussions, though less common, are a growing concern in con-
105	tact sports, with rugby union players experiencing concussion rates between 8.2 and
106	16.11 per 1000 h of activity, Gaelic football players 5.21 per 1000 h, and football players

110	between 2.08 and 4.04 per 1000 activity events.8 Beyond the biological and environmen-
111	tal factors inﬂuencing predisposition and injury risk, it is important to consider the sig-
112	niﬁcant economic impact of sports injuries. A recent literature review revealed that,
113	despite methodological heterogeneity, studies consistently report substantial direct and
114	indirect costs associated with sports injuries, including medical expenses, income loss,
115	and reduced quality of life.9 For example, a study conducted in Switzerland analyzing
116	702 injuries in amateur football estimated an average cost of €4030 per injury, with costs
117	reaching up to €8190 for players over 30 competing in speciﬁc amateur leagues.10 These
118	ﬁgures illustrate the considerable burden sports injuries place on healthcare systems and
119	individuals, underscoring the urgent need for effective prevention and management strat-
120	egies tailored to the speciﬁc demands of each sport.
121	    Research has increasingly focused on the genetic basis of athletic status. For example,
122	a genome-wide linkage scan involving 700 pairs of British dizygotic twins estimated that
123	approximately 66% of the variance in athlete status could be explained by genetic factors,
124	according to the speciﬁc assumptions of the twin study design. This estimate, however,
125	varies across sport disciplines and depends on the criteria used to deﬁne athlete status.11
126	Several studies have also reported associations between speciﬁc genetic polymorphisms
127	and the predisposition to distinct categories of sports-related injuries, such as those affect-
128	ing muscle tissue, bone structure, and concussions, which differ substantially in their
129	underlying pathophysiology.1,12–16 Genetic susceptibility is most often investigated
130	through the analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), the most prevalent
131	form of genetic variation in the human genome. Other types of variants, including inser-
132	tion–deletion polymorphisms, have likewise been implicated in modulating injury risk
133	and recovery, potentially through effects on gene expression or protein function. Each
134	SNP may give rise to distinct genotypes, such as homozygous (e.g., AA or TT) or het-
135	erozygous (e.g., AT) combinations. These genotypes can inﬂuence gene expression or
136	protein function and are frequently examined to investigate associations with athletic per-
137	formance, injury risk, or recovery potential.17
138	    Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation and microRNAs (miRNAs), modulate
139	gene activity and are inﬂuenced by exercise and environmental factors. MicroRNAs are a class
140	of small, noncoding RNA molecules approximately 20–22 nucleotides long that regulate gene
141	expression at the posttranscriptional level by binding to messenger RNAs and promoting their
142	degradation or inhibiting their translation. They are key regulators of biological processes,
143	including tissue repair, inﬂammation, and muscle regeneration, thereby impacting injury sus-
144	ceptibility and recovery dynamics. In the context of concussions, they are involved in neuroin-
145	ﬂammatory responses and neuronal repair. Understanding these genetic and epigenetic
146	contributions enables sports medicine professionals to identify athletes at higher risk of injury,
147	to personalize training and recovery protocols based on each athlete’s genetic and epigenetic
148	proﬁle, which may inﬂuence muscle repair capacity, inﬂammatory responses, bone remodel-
149	ing, and neurological recovery. This could involve aligning training variables, such as inten-
150	sity, type (e.g., explosive vs. endurance emphasis), volume, and recovery duration, with the
151	athlete’s speciﬁc biological predispositions. For example, individuals with SNPs or miRNA
152	expression patterns linked to slower tissue repair or higher inﬂammation might beneﬁt from
153	more conservative return-to-play timelines, targeted anti-inﬂammatory strategies, longer rest

240	Genetic polymorphisms related to muscle injuries in athletes
241	Muscle injuries result from damage to muscle ﬁbers, caused by, for example, a contusion
242	(sudden impact) or a strain (excessive tensile force). These injuries often lead to myoﬁber rup-
243	ture, typically near the myotendinous junction.24 Common in sports, they can be classiﬁed by
244	mechanism, location, severity, and recurrence frequency.25 Research has shown associations
245	between various genetic variants and susceptibility to muscle injuries in athletes (Table 1),
246	focusing on genes involved in muscle structure, regeneration, energy metabolism, contrac-
247	tion, and the regulation of inﬂammation and oxidative stress response.26,27 This review iden-
248	tiﬁed 17 genes and 21 polymorphisms linked to muscle injuries.

251	Genes, muscle structure, and integrity in athletes
252	Intensive exercise can induce changes in muscle ﬁber structure and organization, which
253	are inﬂuenced by several genes associated with muscle composition, function, and
254	 6                                                                       Science Progress 108(4)

256	
257	particularly muscle contraction. These genetic variants enable athletes to adapt better to
258	training while resisting muscle injuries. Collagen plays a vital role in regulating collagen ﬁbril
259	formation and organization in various connective tissues, including skeletal muscle.27 Genetic
260	variants inﬂuencing muscle structure and integrity are crucial for maintaining the stability and
261	elongation of muscle ﬁbers. One signiﬁcant variant is the R577X or C577 T polymorphism
262	(rs1815739) in the ACTN3 gene, where arginine (R) is replaced by a stop codon (X) at position
263	577. This polymorphism is also referred to using the nucleotide nomenclature, with
264	R = C and X = T. Individuals with the homozygous XX genotype lack α-actinin-3, making
265	them more prone to muscle injuries.29 Whereas those with the RR or RX genotypes produce
266	α-actinin-3, with higher expression in RR individuals.48 According to the literature, results on
267	ACTN3 are not uniform across studies. Six studies reported no association between the
268	ACTN3 polymorphism and muscle injuries, particularly in football and rugby
269	players,16,49–51 as well as in runners and endurance athletes.48,52 However, a larger group
270	of studies has reported associations between R577X polymorphism of the ACTN3 gene
271	and an increased predisposition to muscle injuries in football players,26,28,29,33,35,50,53,54
272	half marathon runners,55 and marathon runners.56 This vulnerability is attributed to increased
273	instability of the Z discs and, consequently, the sarcomere, resulting in excessive polymeriza-
274	tion of actin ﬁlaments. This disruption can compromise the effective transmission of muscle
275	contraction signals and lead to a decrease in the force generated by muscle ﬁbers.53
276	    Among the studies that found this association, the X allele is associated with an
277	increased risk of muscle injuries compared to the R allele.28,33,34 Moreover, the XX geno-
278	type appears linked to longer recovery times35 and lower match performance values than
279	RR players..53 In contrast, the R allele is signiﬁcantly more prevalent among female
280	athletes with muscle injuries in sports such as football, softball, basketball, and badmin-
281	ton (p = 0.04),36 and also in those with injuries related to endurance running training.56
282	The recent narrative review by Kahya and Taheri, which provides a stratiﬁed synthesis of
283	genetic markers by sport type and gene function, supports the association of ACTN3
284	R577X polymorphism with soft-tissue injury risk, particularly in strength- and
285	endurance-based disciplines.57 Additionally, the R allele of ACTN3 has been shown to
286	protect football players from developing muscle injuries29 and is linked to a decrease
287	in serum creatine kinase (CK) levels.55 Pimenta et al. showed that CK levels (4 h after
288	exercise), cortisol levels (2 h after exercise), and alpha-actin levels (postexercise) were
289	generally higher in Brazilian professional football players with the ACTN3 XX genotype.
290	However, the results also showed that the R allele was signiﬁcantly associated with
291	higher levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6).54 Finally, a marginal association was detected for
292	ACTN3 rs1815739, where athletes with the R allele seem more likely to experience mus-
293	cle pain (MP) after exercise than those with the XX genotype.58 A systematic review
294	found that the XX genotype is associated with sports injuries, particularly among elite
295	athletes.59 Overall, ACTN3 polymorphisms appear to inﬂuence injury risk through
296	both structural mechanisms (Z-disc and sarcomere instability) and biochemical pathways
297	(CK, cortisol, IL-6). These effects are modulated by athlete sex, sport type, and recovery
298	response. This integrative view reconciles divergent ﬁndings across studies and suggests
299	that ACTN3 could serve as a practical marker to guide personalized training loads and
300	recovery strategies.

364	Genes, inﬂammatory response, and muscle repair mechanisms in athletes
365	The inﬂammatory phase is the ﬁrst stage of muscle repair, characterized by the disorgan-
366	ization of myoﬁbrils and vascular ruptures following mechanical or metabolic stress.65
367	This structural disruption leads to the release of pro-inﬂammatory mediators, such as
368	cytokines and chemokines, into the extracellular space. These signals attract immune
369	cells to the site of injury and contribute to the formation of a hematoma.66 This process
370	also activates proteolytic enzymes, stimulates cell proliferation and migration, and initi-
371	ates the repair of damaged cell membranes. In addition, calcium inﬂux triggers several
372	intracellular signaling pathways, such as NF-κB, MAPK, PI3 K/Akt, and JAK/STAT,
373	that facilitate the removal of cellular debris and promote tissue regeneration.67 In this con-
374	text, genetic polymorphisms may inﬂuence the inﬂammatory response and the extent of
375	muscle recovery. For example, the CCR2 gene variants rs768539 and rs3918358 have
376	been associated with reduced pre-exercise strength, impaired strength recovery, and
377	increased pain perception in some individuals.37 Furthermore, no association was found
378	between the rs768539 polymorphism of the CCR2 gene and hamstring injuries in football
379	players.47 CCR2 polymorphisms appear to modulate the intensity of the inﬂammatory
380	response and the efﬁciency of muscle recovery, although their impact on actual injury
381	risk remains uncertain. Similarly, the GG genotype of the CNTF gene (rs2515362) has
382	been associated with better adaptability to strength training, potentially leading to greater
383	muscle gains, improved resistance to injuries, and enhanced fatigue tolerance in sports
384	school students.38 This suggests that CNTF variants may act as modulators of neuromus-
385	cular adaptation, with implications for both performance and resilience to injury. In add-
386	ition, a study conducted among football players revealed a signiﬁcant association
387	between the rs9290271 polymorphism of the LIF gene and muscle injuries and recovery
388	time.43 These ﬁndings indicate that LIF polymorphisms could inﬂuence tissue repair
389	dynamics, potentially serving as markers for predicting recovery duration after muscle
390	injuries. Finally, the T allele of the HGF gene (rs5745678) seems to offer protection
391	against severe injuries, likely by enhancing HGF-mediated muscle regeneration pro-
392	cesses such as activation of muscle stem cells, promotion of anti-inﬂammatory macro-
393	phage phenotypes, and inhibition of ﬁbrosis, which collectively contribute to faster
394	recovery times.68 Furthermore, the CA/AA genotypes (rs5745697) are linked to minor

403	Genes and muscle energy metabolism in athletes
404	Energetic regulation plays an important role in maintaining cellular energy homeostasis,
405	thus ensuring better muscle contraction function and movement. The accumulation of
406	waste products can damage cells and make them more susceptible to injuries during high-
407	intensity activities, which is particularly noticeable in certain athletes. This is due to dis-
408	ruptions caused by genetic variants that affect energy metabolism, as well as oxidative
409	stress related to waste accumulation and a decrease in the transport of metabolites and
410	energy substrates.15,16,33 The polymorphism c.34C > T (rs17602729) of the AMPD1
411	gene has been extensively studied in the context of sports injuries. Research has shown
412	that individuals carrying the T allele, especially those with the TT genotype, are more
413	likely to develop metabolic myopathies characterized by exercise-induced muscle symp-
414	toms such as early fatigue, cramps, and myalgias. These symptoms increase their injury
415	risk, particularly in demanding sports like football.15,16,33 Furthermore, athletes with the
416	TT genotype exhibit decreased exercise capacity and cardiorespiratory responses, as well
417	as a limited response to endurance training, which may also contribute to an increased
418	risk of injury. Studies indicate that football players with the CC genotype of the
419	AMPD1 gene experience fewer ankle and knee injuries and play more matches than those
420	expressing a T allele. This is true for both professional and amateur football players, sug-
421	gesting that the CC genotype may offer protection against injuries.15,16,33 This link
422	between the AMPD1 polymorphism and sports injuries is particularly relevant for endur-
423	ance athletes, where optimal muscle metabolism is essential for injury prevention.52
424	Overall, AMPD1 polymorphisms appear to shape individual susceptibility to muscle
425	injuries by inﬂuencing energy metabolism efﬁciency and tolerance to high physical
426	demands. Moreover, the AA genotype of the gene MCT1 (rs1049434) is associated
427	with a signiﬁcant increase in muscle injuries in elite football players compared to the
428	TT genotype.44 Furthermore, Italian football players with the TT genotype have a signiﬁ-
429	cantly higher percentage of lean body mass than those with the AA genotype, suggesting
430	that the T allele is linked to better body composition in young athletes.45 Additionally,
431	another study conducted on Italian football players revealed that carriers of the T allele
432	have a protective effect against muscle injuries.29 One study reported a transmission dis-
433	tortion, meaning in this case a deviation from the Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium at the
434	population level, of the MCT1 rs1049434 polymorphism, with an overrepresentation of
435	the T allele among elite Polish athletes, including both endurance athletes (3000 m, mara-
436	thon, cross-country skiing, swimming, triathlon, and rowing) and power/speed athletes
437	(100–400 m sprint, weightlifting, and powerlifting).69 However, no signiﬁcant difference
438	was observed in the allele distribution of the A/T polymorphism (rs1049434) of the
439	MCT1 gene between athletes and the control group, suggesting that this polymorphism
440	may not inﬂuence muscle injury susceptibility in young athletes preparing for the
441	Turkish Youth Championship.70 Taken together, MCT1 polymorphisms may contribute

449	Genes, cardiovascular, and muscle regulation in athletes
450	Cardiovascular and muscular regulation is essential for maintaining muscle integrity by
451	regulating oxygen supply and blood transport through arteries and veins. Genetic variants
452	have been associated with vasodilation issues, which can lead to a decrease in blood pres-
453	sure. The imbalance in this regulation causes muscle fatigue and the accumulation of
454	metabolic waste. This makes muscles more susceptible to injuries, especially during
455	training. Genetic variants play a key role in cardiovascular and muscular regulation.71,72
456	For example, motor activity induces dynamic changes in ACE gene expression in rats,
457	with bioinformatics analysis linking these shifts to cardiovascular regulation and electro-
458	lyte balance during endurance exercise.73 A common genetic variation known as the ACE
459	I/D polymorphism (rs1799752) alters the expression of the ACE enzyme and may affect
460	cardiovascular health. This polymorphism results from the insertion (I) or deletion (D) of
461	a 287 bp Alu sequence within intron 16 of the ACE gene, resulting in three distinct gen-
462	otypes: II, ID, and DD.74 Increased activity of the ACE enzyme, often associated with the
463	D allele, promotes the production of angiotensin II while decreasing the half-life of
464	bradykinin. This dynamic may inﬂuence inﬂammatory responses following muscle
465	injury, given that angiotensin II and bradykinin play signiﬁcant roles in inﬂammation.75
466	Sierra et al. have suggested a link between ACE I/D gene polymorphisms and suscepti-
467	bility to postexercise muscle injuries, particularly sport-related muscle damage (SRMD).
468	These polymorphisms could inﬂuence sensitivity to such damage by modulating the
469	inﬂammatory response.30 According to research, several studies have highlighted the
470	association of the D allele of the ACE I/D polymorphism with a lower risk of muscle
471	injuries and its protective role against these injuries.29–31 Other studies have reported a
472	correlation between the D allele and lower CK levels,32 a marker of muscle damage, fol-
473	lowing intense efforts such as triathlons55 and marathons.30 Conversely, another study
474	found that athletes with the ID genotype had a higher incidence of sports injuries com-
475	pared to those with the DD and II genotypes.76 Moreover, an interaction between poly-
476	morphisms was observed: the combination of the X allele of the ACTN3 gene with the II

Abstract
Understanding how genetic and epigenetic factors inﬂuence predisposition, susceptibility,
protection, severity, and recovery potential in sports-related muscle, bone, and brain injuries
is gaining increasing attention, as these injuries represent a major concern for athletes’
health and performance. This narrative review explores the role of speciﬁc genetic variants,
such as those in ACE, ACTN3, AMPD1, VDR, and APOE, in predisposing athletes to injury.
In parallel, the emerging role of microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-133a, miR-208a, and
miR-214 in regulating gene expression related to muscle regeneration, inﬂammation, and
neuroprotection, is highlighted. These small noncoding RNAs are inﬂuenced by environ-
mental stimuli such as sports activity and training, and may serve as promising biomarkers

Introduction
The predisposition to injury and sports performance is primarily determined by intrinsic
biological traits, including genetic polymorphisms that inﬂuence muscle structure, bone
density, and neuromuscular function. While training and other extrinsic factors can
modulate injury risk, they do not deﬁne the baseline predisposition, which is rooted in
these intrinsic characteristics.
    The Healthy Injury-Free Adolescent Athletes study has shown that multiple factors,
including biomechanical, environmental, and psychosocial aspects, contribute signiﬁ-
cantly to injury risk in young athletes.1 Similarly, studies on Olympic athletes have
demonstrated that elite-level performance tends to run in families, emphasizing the
important contribution of genetic background.2 Foundational studies further suggest
that up to 60–70% of the variability in physiological adaptations to physical activity
(such as VO2max and strength gains) and injury susceptibility may be explained by gen-
etic factors.3 Engaging in intense physical activity comes with an increased risk of injur-
ies, the nature and severity of which vary depending on the sport. Indeed, each sport has a
speciﬁc risk proﬁle, related to its unique physical and technical demands. Nearly 70% of
track and ﬁeld athletes experience injuries per season.4 Lower limb injuries are extremely
common in certain sports, affecting 50% of athletes participating in football, marathon,
triathlon, gymnastics (female), basketball, pole vaulting, rugby sevens, volleyball
(female), handball, and tennis.5 Among these injuries, muscular injuries such as ham-
string strains are particularly prevalent; for instance, professional footballers experience
a 20% hamstring injury rate per season, with 20% of these progressing to a chronic stage.6
Stress fractures and stress reactions, while less frequent, pose a greater challenge due to
their longer recovery periods, with athletes requiring on average 67.4 days (± 73.1) to
return to full training for stress reactions, and up to 199 days (± 205.2) for stress frac-
tures.7 In comparison, concussions, though less common, are a growing concern in con-
tact sports, with rugby union players experiencing concussion rates between 8.2 and
16.11 per 1000 h of activity, Gaelic football players 5.21 per 1000 h, and football players
 Marrouh et al.                                                                                  3


between 2.08 and 4.04 per 1000 activity events.8 Beyond the biological and environmen-
tal factors inﬂuencing predisposition and injury risk, it is important to consider the sig-
niﬁcant economic impact of sports injuries. A recent literature review revealed that,
despite methodological heterogeneity, studies consistently report substantial direct and
indirect costs associated with sports injuries, including medical expenses, income loss,
and reduced quality of life.9 For example, a study conducted in Switzerland analyzing
702 injuries in amateur football estimated an average cost of €4030 per injury, with costs
reaching up to €8190 for players over 30 competing in speciﬁc amateur leagues.10 These
ﬁgures illustrate the considerable burden sports injuries place on healthcare systems and
individuals, underscoring the urgent need for effective prevention and management strat-
egies tailored to the speciﬁc demands of each sport.
    Research has increasingly focused on the genetic basis of athletic status. For example,
a genome-wide linkage scan involving 700 pairs of British dizygotic twins estimated that
approximately 66% of the variance in athlete status could be explained by genetic factors,
according to the speciﬁc assumptions of the twin study design. This estimate, however,
varies across sport disciplines and depends on the criteria used to deﬁne athlete status.11
Several studies have also reported associations between speciﬁc genetic polymorphisms
and the predisposition to distinct categories of sports-related injuries, such as those affect-
ing muscle tissue, bone structure, and concussions, which differ substantially in their
underlying pathophysiology.1,12–16 Genetic susceptibility is most often investigated
through the analysis of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), the most prevalent
form of genetic variation in the human genome. Other types of variants, including inser-
tion–deletion polymorphisms, have likewise been implicated in modulating injury risk
and recovery, potentially through effects on gene expression or protein function. Each
SNP may give rise to distinct genotypes, such as homozygous (e.g., AA or TT) or het-
erozygous (e.g., AT) combinations. These genotypes can inﬂuence gene expression or
protein function and are frequently examined to investigate associations with athletic per-
formance, injury risk, or recovery potential.17
    Epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation and microRNAs (miRNAs), modulate
gene activity and are inﬂuenced by exercise and environmental factors. MicroRNAs are a class
of small, noncoding RNA molecules approximately 20–22 nucleotides long that regulate gene
expression at the posttranscriptional level by binding to messenger RNAs and promoting their
degradation or inhibiting their translation. They are key regulators of biological processes,
including tissue repair, inﬂammation, and muscle regeneration, thereby impacting injury sus-
ceptibility and recovery dynamics. In the context of concussions, they are involved in neuroin-
ﬂammatory responses and neuronal repair. Understanding these genetic and epigenetic
contributions enables sports medicine professionals to identify athletes at higher risk of injury,
to personalize training and recovery protocols based on each athlete’s genetic and epigenetic
proﬁle, which may inﬂuence muscle repair capacity, inﬂammatory responses, bone remodel-
ing, and neurological recovery. This could involve aligning training variables, such as inten-
sity, type (e.g., explosive vs. endurance emphasis), volume, and recovery duration, with the
athlete’s speciﬁc biological predispositions. For example, individuals with SNPs or miRNA
expression patterns linked to slower tissue repair or higher inﬂammation might beneﬁt from
more conservative return-to-play timelines, targeted anti-inﬂammatory strategies, longer rest

    To our knowledge, this narrative review is the ﬁrst to integrate genetic and epigenetic
evidence related to muscle, bone, and concussion injuries in athletes. It consolidates cur-

and discusses their potential applications for personalized injury prevention strategies in
sports medicine.

A nonsystematic search of the scientiﬁc literature was conducted in PubMed, Scopus,
Web of Science, EBSCO, and Google Scholar, covering publications up to 2025.
Keywords included: “sports injuries”, “muscle injuries”, “stress fractures”, “concus-
sions”, “genetic polymorphisms”, “sports genetics”, and “miRNA”, combined with “ath-
letes”, “susceptibility”, and “epigenetics”. Additional searches used related terms and
synonyms (e.g., “soft tissue injuries”, “bone stress injury”, “traumatic brain injury”,"gene
variants”, “non-coding RNA”) to maximize coverage. Eligible publications included ori-
ginal research articles, narrative or systematic reviews, focused on human studies involv-
ing athletes or physically active individuals. Since this is not a systematic review, article
selection was based on relevance to the topic, scientiﬁc value, and contribution to
