444	
445	DISCUSSION
446	                                           TE
447	        This study used a dataset of over 200 NCAA Division 1 college athletes to determine the
448	
449	
450	
451	
452	                      EP
453	relationship between lower extremity muscle volumes and CMJ performance. After accounting
454	
455	for sex and sport, vastus lateralis muscle volume was identified to be a major contributor to both
456	
457	jump height and peak power, underscoring its key role in vertical jump performance. In addition
458	
459	to the vastus lateralis, which was the only muscle common to both regression models, the jump
460	
461	           C
462	height model included the rectus femoris, while the peak power model retained the soleus,
463	
464	gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps femoris long head. The differing muscle candidates
465	
466	C
467	in the two models likely reflect the distinct features of each CMJ metric: jump height reflects
468	
469	force over time (impulse, N·s) while peak power reflects the rapid generation of force (N·m/s)
470	
471	A
472	(17).
473	
474	
475	
476	
477	                                                 8
478	
479	
480	
481	Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
482	 Importance of the Quadriceps in Jump Performance
483	
484	       Quadricep muscles facilitate extension of the knee, providing the primary vertical
485	
486	propulsion for the lower extremities during jumping (8, 18). Prior studies assessing a select
487	
488	number of lower extremity muscles have shown relationships between quadriceps strength and
489	
490	thickness and jump performance (10, 19). In our analysis, vastus lateralis was strongly associated
491	
492	with both jump height and peak power when included amongst an expanded pool of lower
493	
494	                                                                D
495	extremity muscles. The vastus lateralis was highly correlated with the vastus medialis and vastus
496	
497	intermedius volumes (Supplemental Table 4, Supplemental Digital Content,
498	
499	
500	
501	                                            TE
502	http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), suggesting it may be representative of overall quadriceps
503	
504	muscle volume. In addition, the vastus lateralis is the largest of the quadriceps muscles, making
505	
506	it particularly influential in vertical propulsion during jumping (20, 21). Given these findings,
507	
508	
509	
510	
511	                       EP
512	targeting hypertrophy of the vastus lateralis, and by extension the quadriceps, may be a
513	
514	promising strategy to enhance jump performance, although longitudinal studies are needed to
515	
516	establish a causal relationship.
517	
518	       Besides the vastus lateralis, both jump height and peak power regression models
519	
520	           C
521	contained additional unique muscles, though their influences were less pronounced. In the jump
522	
523	height model, the rectus femoris was the only other muscle retained. Given that it crosses both
524	
525	C
526	the hip and knee and undergoes minimal length change during the CMJ, the rectus femoris may
527	
528	primarily transfer energy between joints rather than significantly contribute to vertical propulsion
529	
530	A
531	(22, 23). However, because it spans both joints, greater rectus femoris volume may allow for
532	
533	more effective force transmission from the hip to the knee during push-off and help transfer
534	
535	energy during rapid knee extension. Increased muscle volume may also reflect adaptations in
536	
537	muscle architecture (e.g., greater physiological cross‑sectional area and stiffness) that enable the
538	
539	
540	                                                 9
541	
542	
543	
544	Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
545	 rectus femoris to sustain and transmit higher forces and enhance inter‑joint energy transfer
546	
547	during the CMJ. In the peak power model, soleus, gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps
548	
549	femoris long head were retained alongside the vastus lateralis. The soleus primarily contributes
550	
551	to vertical ground reaction force through ankle plantarflexion and indirectly assists knee
552	
553	extension through closed-chain mechanics, though it has less mechanical advantage at the knee
554	
555	than the vastus lateralis in vertical jump (24, 25). Although the gluteus medius and adductor
556	
557	                                                               D
558	magnus aid in hip extension, their activation patterns suggest their primary role may be
559	
560	stabilizing the hip joint, thereby optimizing force transfer through the lower extremity during the
561	
562	CMJ (25).
563	                                           TE
564	       Conversely, our findings showed that smaller biceps femoris long head muscle volume
565	
566	was related to greater jump power. An interaction effect was observed between vastus lateralis
567	
568	
569	
570	
571	                      EP
572	and biceps femoris long head muscle volumes in our post hoc analysis (Supplemental Table 5,
573	
574	Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), demonstrating that a possible
575	
576	trade-off between muscle volume distribution and peak jump power may exist. This finding
577	
578	highlights the possibility that greater muscle size may not always be beneficial toward the task of
579	
580	            C
581	interest, in this case the CMJ. As such, understanding how specific muscle size distributions
582	
583	impact lower extremity biomechanics and power output provides deeper insights into optimizing
584	
585	C
586	jump mechanics.
587	
588	Sport Differences
589	
590	A      On average, hockey players jumped the highest (Table 1), likely reflecting their sport-
591	
592	specific demands, which require consistent, powerful hip and knee extension for skating strides
593	
594	(26). Male hockey players also had notably larger normalized quadriceps volumes, particularly in
595	
596	the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis, which may also explain their greater jump heights
597	
598	
599	                                                10
600	
601	
602	
603	Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
604	 (Supplemental Table 6, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362).
605	
606	Basketball players, despite frequently jumping during sport, demonstrated lower jump heights
607	
608	compared to hockey, football, and soccer athletes. Our findings also indicated that athletes with
609	
610	larger quadricep muscle volumes relative to body size generally produced greater peak power.
611	
612	This relationship was most pronounced in male hockey players.
613	
614	Limitations
615	
616	                                                                D
617	       As this study involved high-level collegiate athletes at a single institution, the findings
618	
619	may not be fully generalizable to recreational, high school, or professional populations. Second,
620	
621	
622	
623	                                           TE
624	while our models identified muscle volumes significantly associated with CMJ performance,
625	
626	these muscles may not contribute similarly to other movements required in each specific sport.
627	
628	Third, given the cross-sectional study design, there is no direct evidence to support that training
629	
630	
631	
632	
633	                      EP
634	for hypertrophy in these identified muscle groups will result in better jump performance. Fourth,
635	
636	because this was an exploratory analysis, it is important to note that our use of multiple
637	
638	regression procedures (including backward selection and a post hoc interaction test) may have
639	
640	increased the risk of type I error. Lastly, the measurement of muscle volume provides unique
641	
642	           C
643	insights into characterizing individual muscle contribution to CMJ, but is not a direct measure of
644	
645	muscle strength.
646	
647	C
648	CONCLUSIONS
649	
650	       We identified that quadriceps muscle volume, particularly the vastus lateralis, was most
651	
652	A
653	strongly associated with CMJ height and peak power in elite athletes after accounting for sex and
654	
655	sport. While other muscles, such as the gluteus medius, rectus femoris, biceps femoris long head,
656	
657	adductor magnus, and soleus, were related to jump performance, their influence was less
658	
659	pronounced. These findings highlight the critical role of the quadriceps in vertical jump
660	
661	
662	                                                 11
663	
664

667	 performance and suggest that strength and conditioning and rehabilitation programs may
668	
669	consider targeting quadriceps hypertrophy to improve vertical jump performance.

The Role of Lower-Limb Muscle Volumes in Vertical Jump Performance in NCAA

Division 1 Athletes

Dan O’Brien, Naoaki Ito, Stephanie Kliethermes, and Bryan Heiderscheit

Department of Orthopedics and Rehabilitation, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI

Running Title: MUSCLE VOLUMES AND VERTICAL JUMP PERFORMANCE
                                                               D
Address for correspondence: Bryan Heiderscheit, 1685 Highland Ave, Madison, WI 53706;



                                           TE
Phone: (608) 263-5428; E-mail: heiderscheit@wisc.edu

Conflict of Interest and Funding Source: This work was supported by the University of

Wisconsin Department of Orthopedics and Rehabilitation Freedom of Movement and Pilot




                      EP
Award programs and the National Football League (NFL). The authors would like to

acknowledge the Sports Medicine staff in the University of Wisconsin-Madison Division of

Athletics for their commitment to the welfare of the student-athletes and contributions to the

Badger Athletic Performance program. Bryan Heiderscheit is an advisory board member for

          C
Springbok Analytics (stock options). Stephanie Kliethermes is a statistical consultant for

Springbok Analytics. The remaining authors declare that they have no competing interests.

C
A
                                                1



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 ABSTRACT

Introduction/Purpose: This study examined the relationship between lower extremity muscle

volumes and countermovement jump (CMJ) performance in 207 (43 female, 164 male) NCAA

Division I collegiate basketball, football, hockey, and soccer athletes. The primary aim was to

determine which combination of lower extremity muscle volumes was most strongly associated

with CMJ performance across a large subset of high-level college athletes. Methods: Athletes

                                                                D
underwent bilateral MRI scans, and muscle volumes were quantified using machine-learning-

based auto-segmentation. CMJ height (cm) and peak power (W/kg) were measured using dual



                                            TE
force plates. Backward selection regression analyses determined muscle combinations that best

explained variance in jump performance after adjusting for sex and sport. Results: Vastus

lateralis muscle volume was related to both jump height (β = 0.36, p < 0.01) and peak power (β =




                      EP
0.41, p < 0.01). In addition to the vastus lateralis, the jump height model retained rectus femoris,

and the peak power model retained soleus, gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps femoris

long head. The differing muscle candidates in the two models likely reflect the distinct features

of each CMJ metric: jump height reflects force over time (impulse, N·s) while peak power

           C
reflects the rapid generation of force (N·m/s). Sport-specific differences emerged, with hockey

and football athletes displaying greater jump heights and generating greater peak power when

C
compared to basketball players. Male athletes outperformed females in both jump metrics.

Conclusions: These findings, derived from over 200 NCAA Division I athletes, highlight the

A
crucial role of the quadriceps in CMJ performance in high-level athletes. Strength and

conditioning and rehabilitation programs may consider targeting quadriceps hypertrophy to

improve vertical jump performance. Key Words: COUNTERMOVEMENT JUMP,

MAGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING, VASTUS LATERALIS, QUADRICEPS


                                                 2



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 INTRODUCTION

       The ability to generate force and power through the lower extremities during athletic

tasks such as jumping is a critical determinant of performance (1–3). The countermovement

jump (CMJ) is a foundational movement for various sport-specific skills and is widely used by

sports medicine and science practitioners as a time-efficient testing method for assessing lower-

body power, performance, and readiness for return to play from injury (4–6).

                                                                D
       Larger muscle size is known to relate to greater force and power production (7, 8).

However, traditional imaging methods for quantifying muscle volumes to assess function are



                                            TE
time-intensive, requiring manual segmentation and extensive processing, limiting the scope of

investigations to key muscle groups and smaller sample sizes. As a result, prior research

examining the relationship between muscle size and jump performance has primarily focused on




                      EP
a select few muscles, particularly the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and lateral gastrocnemius as

predictors of jump performance (8–10). Further, most studies have strictly investigated the

muscle morphology (e.g. anatomical cross-sectional area or thickness) and architecture (e.g.,

pennation angle, fascicle length, and physiological cross-sectional area) of large, primary

           C
muscles, but less is known about the role of other muscles (2, 8, 11). Traditional approaches to

imaging may overlook contributions from other lower extremity muscles and limit our

C
understanding of how these muscles influence jump performance.

       Advancements in machine learning technology have enabled the rapid measurement of

A
muscle volumes from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, offering the opportunity to

quantify various lower extremity muscle volumes. This technology has demonstrated utility in

assessing associations between muscle volume and sprint and vertical jump performance in male

basketball players and untrained individuals, as well as persistent muscle atrophy post-surgery


                                                 3



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 and in elite athlete populations (12, 13). This study aimed to determine which combination of

lower extremity muscle volumes was most strongly associated with CMJ performance across a

large subset of high-level college athletes.

METHODS

       This cross-sectional study included a cohort of National Collegiate Athletic Association

(NCAA) Division 1 American football, basketball, ice hockey, and soccer athletes from a single

                                                                 D
institution. Before their competitive season, athletes completed CMJ testing on force plates and

underwent bilateral lower extremity MRI scans. All athletes provided informed consent for the



                                               TE
use of their CMJ and MRI data as part of their respective parent studies, each of which was

approved by the University of Wisconsin–Madison Health Sciences IRB. Athletes were eligible

for inclusion if they were cleared to participate in sport activities without limitation in practice




                       EP
and games at the time of data collection and had both CMJ and MRI data available and collected

within four months of each other.

Jump Performance

       Athletes performed bilateral maximum effort CMJs on portable, dual force platforms that

           C
measured vertical forces at a sampling rate of 800 Hz, with the software’s internal filtering

applied (Leonardo Mechanograph; Novotec Medical, Pforzheim, Germany). Athletes started

C
with one foot on each force plate and hands placed on their hips. Athletes were instructed to

“jump as high as possible” while maintaining their hands on their hips throughout the jump. A

A
jump trial was considered successful if athletes landed with one foot on each force plate and

maintained their balance. Athletes completed up to three successful trials. If a trial was

unsuccessful, the athlete repeated the attempt, up to a maximum of five total jump trials per

testing session.


                                                  4



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 Quantifying Muscle Volume

       Athletes from all sports underwent MRI of the lumbopelvic region and bilateral lower

extremities using a 1.5T SIGNA Voyager Air Edition Mobile MRI (GE HealthCare, Chicago, IL,

USA) or a 3-T scanner (SIGNA Premier [GE Healthcare]) equipped with a flexible surface coil.

Imaging was performed continuously from the 12th thoracic vertebra to below the ankle joint in

sets of 40 scans to capture the entire field of view. Axial multislice 2-dimensional fast spoiled

                                                                D
gradient recalled echo (FSPGR) sequences were utilized, with parameters optimized to maximize

the muscle signal and minimize the fat signal (repetition time/echo time: 839 ms/4.35 ms; field



                                           TE
of view: 500 × 344 mm; matrix: 256 × 176; voxel size: 2 × 2 × 5 mm). In all instances, the

acquired images were processed using automated machine-learning-based auto-segmentation

algorithms to obtain 38 individual muscle volumes for each limb (Springbok Analytics,




                       EP
Charlottesville, VA), which has demonstrated repeatability comparable with interobserver

variability (14, 15). Muscle volumes were then normalized to athletes' body mass and height

(mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹) (14).

Muscle and Jump Variable Selection

           C
       Jump height (cm) and peak power (W) were the primary variables of interest in the CMJ.

Peak power during the concentric takeoff phase was assessed (i.e., the period of upward

C
propulsion until foot-off), and jump height was calculated based on impulse momentum from the

proprietary Leonardo Mechanograph software. Data from the trial with the highest jump height

A
were extracted, and takeoff peak power from the same trial was normalized to body mass (W/kg)

to allow for comparison across athletes. Given that the joint movements responsible for the CMJ

primarily occur in the sagittal plane, we only included the 23 lower extremity muscles

responsible for flexion and extension at the hip, knee, and ankle as candidate variables for


                                                 5



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 analysis (Figure 1). Since the CMJ is a bilateral task, we summed the muscle volumes from both

sides to obtain a single volume for each muscle to use for analysis.

Statistical Analyses

          Descriptive statistics (mean ± standard deviation) were calculated for height, weight,

jump height (cm), normalized peak power (W/kg), and normalized muscle volumes

(mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹). Multiple regression analyses with backwards selection were conducted to

                                                                 D
determine the combination of muscle volumes that best explained variance in jump height and

peak power. Both sex (male, female) and sport (basketball, football, hockey, soccer) were forced


                                             TE
into the model as potential covariates. The analysis began with a full model that included all 23

muscle volumes. The least contributing muscle was removed at each iteration based on the

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), calculated to penalize additional candidate muscles and




                        EP
reduce overfitting. The process continued until no muscle removed from the model decreased the

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) score by greater than two points (16). Effect estimates (β)

and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) are reported, as well as the unadjusted and adjusted R2

values.

             C
          Given the model findings, a post hoc F-test comparing nested linear models was run as a

separate analysis to test the significance of the interaction between biceps femoris long head and

C
vastus lateralis in the peak power model. Type III ANOVAs were performed on the final

regression models to assess the overall effect of sport. Multicollinearity was assessed using the

A
variance inflation factor (VIF) to identify candidate variables exceeding the threshold of five. All

statistical analyses were performed in R (Version 4.4.1; R Core Team 2024), with the following

packages: broom (v1.0.7), car (v3.1.2), corrplot (v0.92), dplyr (v1.1.4), ggcorrplot (v0.1.4.1),

ggplot2 (v3.5.1), lm.beta (v1.7.2), MASS (v7.3.60.2).


                                                   6



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 RESULTS

       Two hundred and seven collegiate athletes were included in the study (Supplemental

Table 1, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), comprised of 164

males (height: 187.3 ± 7.6 cm, weight: 98.4 ± 20.0 kg) and 43 females (172.0 ± 8.1 cm, 69.5 ±

10.5 kg).

       Following backward selection, the final model for CMJ jump height (Fig. 2;

                                                               D
Supplemental Table 2, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362)

explained 54% of the variance in jump height (R² = 0.56, adjusted R² = 0.54). The model



                                           TE
included the vastus lateralis (estimate [95% CI] = 1.39 [0.91, 1.87], β = 0.36, p < 0.01) and

rectus femoris (1.20 [-0.11, 2.51], β = 0.11, p = 0.07) muscle volumes after adjusting for sex and

sport. A 1 mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹ greater vastus lateralis muscle volume related to a 1.39 [0.91, 1.87] cm




                      EP
higher jump height. A Type III ANOVA indicated a significant main effect of sport (F(3, 200) =

7.68, p < .001). Marginal sport and sex specific regression coefficients were examined relative to

basketball (reference sport) and female (reference sex), and both are adjusted for all other

variables in the model. Hockey (6.63 [3.63, 9.63], β = 0.27, p < 0.01) and football (3.76 [1.26,

            C
6.26], β = 0.22, p < 0.01) were associated with higher jump heights, whereas no difference was

noted in soccer when compared to basketball players. On average, males also jumped higher than

C
females (8.86 [6.52, 11.20], β = 0.43, p < 0.01).

       The final model for peak power (Fig. 2; Supplemental Table 3, Supplemental Digital

A
Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362) explained 71% of the variance in peak power

(R² = 0.72, adjusted R² = 0.71). The model included vastus lateralis (1.67 [1.20, 2.14], β = 0.41,

p < .01), gluteus medius (1.16 [-0.04, 2.36], β = 0.11, p = 0.06), biceps femoris long head (-1.78,

[-3.36, -0.20], β = -0.11, p = 0.03), adductor magnus (0.66 [0.12, 1.20], β = 0.13, p = 0.02), and


                                                    7



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 soleus (1.54 [0.63, 2.44], β = 0.16, p < 0.01) muscle volumes after adjusting for sex and sport. A

1 mL·kg⁻¹·cm⁻¹ greater vastus lateralis muscle volume related to a 1.67 [1.20, 2.14] W/kg higher

peak power. A Type III ANOVA indicated a significant main effect of sport (F(3, 197) = 11.18,

p < .001). Specifically, football (4.49 [2.26, 6.72], p < .01) was associated with greater peak

power compared to basketball players, whereas hockey or soccer, compared to basketball, was

not statistically significant. Males also generated greater peak power than females (8.79 [6.75,

10.83], p < .01).
                                                                D
        Multicollinearity analysis revealed that all muscle volumes in the final models had VIF

values below the threshold of five.

DISCUSSION
                                           TE
        This study used a dataset of over 200 NCAA Division 1 college athletes to determine the




                      EP
relationship between lower extremity muscle volumes and CMJ performance. After accounting

for sex and sport, vastus lateralis muscle volume was identified to be a major contributor to both

jump height and peak power, underscoring its key role in vertical jump performance. In addition

to the vastus lateralis, which was the only muscle common to both regression models, the jump

           C
height model included the rectus femoris, while the peak power model retained the soleus,

gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps femoris long head. The differing muscle candidates

C
in the two models likely reflect the distinct features of each CMJ metric: jump height reflects

force over time (impulse, N·s) while peak power reflects the rapid generation of force (N·m/s)

A
(17).




                                                 8



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 Importance of the Quadriceps in Jump Performance

       Quadricep muscles facilitate extension of the knee, providing the primary vertical

propulsion for the lower extremities during jumping (8, 18). Prior studies assessing a select

number of lower extremity muscles have shown relationships between quadriceps strength and

thickness and jump performance (10, 19). In our analysis, vastus lateralis was strongly associated

with both jump height and peak power when included amongst an expanded pool of lower

                                                                D
extremity muscles. The vastus lateralis was highly correlated with the vastus medialis and vastus

intermedius volumes (Supplemental Table 4, Supplemental Digital Content,



                                            TE
http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), suggesting it may be representative of overall quadriceps

muscle volume. In addition, the vastus lateralis is the largest of the quadriceps muscles, making

it particularly influential in vertical propulsion during jumping (20, 21). Given these findings,




                       EP
targeting hypertrophy of the vastus lateralis, and by extension the quadriceps, may be a

promising strategy to enhance jump performance, although longitudinal studies are needed to

establish a causal relationship.

       Besides the vastus lateralis, both jump height and peak power regression models

           C
contained additional unique muscles, though their influences were less pronounced. In the jump

height model, the rectus femoris was the only other muscle retained. Given that it crosses both

C
the hip and knee and undergoes minimal length change during the CMJ, the rectus femoris may

primarily transfer energy between joints rather than significantly contribute to vertical propulsion

A
(22, 23). However, because it spans both joints, greater rectus femoris volume may allow for

more effective force transmission from the hip to the knee during push-off and help transfer

energy during rapid knee extension. Increased muscle volume may also reflect adaptations in

muscle architecture (e.g., greater physiological cross‑sectional area and stiffness) that enable the


                                                 9



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 rectus femoris to sustain and transmit higher forces and enhance inter‑joint energy transfer

during the CMJ. In the peak power model, soleus, gluteus medius, adductor magnus, and biceps

femoris long head were retained alongside the vastus lateralis. The soleus primarily contributes

to vertical ground reaction force through ankle plantarflexion and indirectly assists knee

extension through closed-chain mechanics, though it has less mechanical advantage at the knee

than the vastus lateralis in vertical jump (24, 25). Although the gluteus medius and adductor

                                                               D
magnus aid in hip extension, their activation patterns suggest their primary role may be

stabilizing the hip joint, thereby optimizing force transfer through the lower extremity during the

CMJ (25).
                                           TE
       Conversely, our findings showed that smaller biceps femoris long head muscle volume

was related to greater jump power. An interaction effect was observed between vastus lateralis




                      EP
and biceps femoris long head muscle volumes in our post hoc analysis (Supplemental Table 5,

Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362), demonstrating that a possible

trade-off between muscle volume distribution and peak jump power may exist. This finding

highlights the possibility that greater muscle size may not always be beneficial toward the task of

            C
interest, in this case the CMJ. As such, understanding how specific muscle size distributions

impact lower extremity biomechanics and power output provides deeper insights into optimizing

C
jump mechanics.

Sport Differences

A      On average, hockey players jumped the highest (Table 1), likely reflecting their sport-

specific demands, which require consistent, powerful hip and knee extension for skating strides

(26). Male hockey players also had notably larger normalized quadriceps volumes, particularly in

the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis, which may also explain their greater jump heights


                                                10



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 (Supplemental Table 6, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MSS/D362).

Basketball players, despite frequently jumping during sport, demonstrated lower jump heights

compared to hockey, football, and soccer athletes. Our findings also indicated that athletes with

larger quadricep muscle volumes relative to body size generally produced greater peak power.

This relationship was most pronounced in male hockey players.

Limitations

                                                                D
       As this study involved high-level collegiate athletes at a single institution, the findings

may not be fully generalizable to recreational, high school, or professional populations. Second,



                                           TE
while our models identified muscle volumes significantly associated with CMJ performance,

these muscles may not contribute similarly to other movements required in each specific sport.

Third, given the cross-sectional study design, there is no direct evidence to support that training




                      EP
for hypertrophy in these identified muscle groups will result in better jump performance. Fourth,

because this was an exploratory analysis, it is important to note that our use of multiple

regression procedures (including backward selection and a post hoc interaction test) may have

increased the risk of type I error. Lastly, the measurement of muscle volume provides unique

           C
insights into characterizing individual muscle contribution to CMJ, but is not a direct measure of

muscle strength.

C
CONCLUSIONS

       We identified that quadriceps muscle volume, particularly the vastus lateralis, was most

A
strongly associated with CMJ height and peak power in elite athletes after accounting for sex and

sport. While other muscles, such as the gluteus medius, rectus femoris, biceps femoris long head,

adductor magnus, and soleus, were related to jump performance, their influence was less

pronounced. These findings highlight the critical role of the quadriceps in vertical jump


                                                 11



Copyright © 2026 by the American College of Sports Medicine
 performance and suggest that strength and conditioning and rehabilitation programs may

consider targeting quadriceps hypertrophy to improve vertical jump performance.

A R T I C L E I N F O                                       A B S T R A C T

Keywords:                                                   Background: Personality traits are increasingly used in athlete selection, yet their predictive validity varies across
Personality traits                                          sports, levels, and cultural contexts. This review identifies which traits best predict performance and through
Athlete selection                                           what mechanisms.
Elite athletes
                                                            Methods: Following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol, we searched five databases through March
Talent identification
Psychological assessment
                                                            2025. Twenty-two cross-sectional studies (N = 4181 athletes; mean age 15–37 years; 14 countries; 18 sports) met
                                                            inclusion criteria. Study quality was assessed via the STROBE checklist.
                                                            Results: Higher conscientiousness and extraversion consistently predicted superior performance (effect sizes
                                                            ~0.26–0.70), while neuroticism was negatively related (β up to − 0.25). Three mechanisms emerged: (1) direct
                                                            neurobiological effects via dopaminergic sensitivity and prefrontal regulation; (2) indirect psychological medi­
                                                            ation through motivation and self-regulation; and (3) contextual moderation by sport type, competitive level,
                                                            and cultural background.
                                                            Conclusions: Conscientiousness, extraversion, and low neuroticism are robust, dynamic predictors of athletic
                                                            success. Incorporating multi-trait assessments tailored to sport and culture can enhance talent identification.
                                                            Future longitudinal, multi-method research with standardized metrics is warranted.

   "abstract":"The review asks which personality traits best predict athletic performance and through what mechanisms. Following PRISMA and a PROSPERO-registered protocol, five databases were searched through March 2025, and 22 cross-sectional studies (N = 4,181 athletes) met the criteria. Higher conscientiousness and extraversion consistently predicted better performance, and neuroticism was negatively related. Three mechanisms are proposed: direct neurobiological effects, indirect psychological mediation, and contextual moderation by sport, level and culture. Conscientiousness, extraversion and low neuroticism are presented as robust predictors that could improve talent identification if assessed alongside sport and cultural context.",
   "tldr":"Across 22 cross-sectional studies of more than 4,000 athletes, higher conscientiousness and extraversion and lower neuroticism went with better performance or selection status. The links are modest, mostly cross-sectional and vary by sport and level, so personality is best used as one input to talent identification rather than a selection rule.",
   "methods":"Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251007053). Five databases (PubMed, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science) were searched on 5 March 2025. Two reviewers screened 2,955 unique records, assessed 423 full texts and included 22 studies. Quality was rated with the STROBE checklist, and results were synthesised narratively because the heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.",
   "findings":"Conscientiousness and extraversion were most often reported as positive predictors of performance, with effect sizes of about 0.26 to 0.70, and neuroticism was negatively related (beta up to -0.25). Some studies reported null associations, for example no significant link between Big Five traits and one-year post-draft performance in baseball. Trait-performance associations were reported as stronger in team sports than in individual sports in one study (interaction p < .05), and the authors describe sport and competitive level as moderators.",
   "limitations":"Most included studies are cross-sectional, several did not control for sex, sport, training history or culture, and personality instruments and performance measures varied widely. The inclusion rule was athlete-only, yet several studies in the review compare athletes with non-athlete groups, and the authors note that publication bias toward null results cannot be ruled out.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use personality profiles as one input alongside physical testing, coach assessment and performance data in talent identification, rather than as a cut-off.  }
}

Six combine tests were normalised as Z-scores against all athletes and against position peers. Spearman correlations and forward-selection regression were used. Of 35 correlations, only two were moderate (r = 0.32 and 0.33), and combine measures explained about 2.6% of the variance in first-year snaps. The authors conclude that the combine lacks predictive ability for first-year game performance and should be used cautiously in draft decisions.",
   "tldr":"In more than 1,500 college players who attended the NFL combine, six physical tests showed weak links to snaps played in later NFL seasons. The combine explained only about 2.6% of first-year playing time, so it should not be the main basis for draft selection.",
   "methods":"Retrospective analysis of public data from pro-football-reference.com and nflcombineresults.com. Players who attended the 2013 to 2017 combines and completed at least one test were included (1,504 analysed). Six events were normalised as average Z-scores overall (avgCZ) and within position (avgPZ). Spearman correlations were run against average snaps in each of five subsequent years, and forward-selection multiple regression was used for the first-year outcome, overall and by position. Institutional review board approval was not required for the secondary public data.",
   "findings":"Of 35 correlations, only two were moderate: avgCZ with year-two snaps (r = 0.320) and avgPZ with year-two snaps (r = 0.332); the rest were weak (r < 0.3). Overall, the regression using vertical jump, bench press and pro-agility explained 2.6% of the variance in first-year average snaps (adjusted R2 = 0.026). Position-specific models explained up to 20.2% of the variance for linebackers (40-yard dash and pro-agility), with smaller values for other positions; no model could be fitted for quarterbacks.",
   "limitations":"The data come from third-party web sources that were not fully verified, not every athlete completed every event, and the analysis did not include the medical history, Wonderlic or position-drill components. Many correlations were tested, so some significant results may be chance findings. The Discussion cites up to 21.9% variance for positional models, while the results report 20.2% for linebackers, so that figure should be checked against the tables.",
   "practicalImplications":"Do not rely on combine physical-test results alone when judging draft prospects, since they showed weak links to snaps played in these data. Position-specific reads may be more informative than a single all-position score, though the explained variance is still small.",
   "athleteDev":"Combine test profiles for linebackers, offensive linemen, running backs and tight ends showed small but identifiable links to early playing time, which may help staff set position-specific testing priorities. The study does not show that improving a test score improves game performance.",
   "rtp":"The study uses healthy draft-eligible players and their playing time, not injury or recovery data, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."
 }
}
